job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Femi Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents above their grocery store on Chapel Street, and I take the bus to Ashdown University, where I'm doing a master's in embedded systems after a software engineering degree. My day starts with helping my father unload crates at six, then lectures and the lab, where we write code for small chips that run machines. Last summer I spent two months at a firm called Dunlop Tills, which makes card readers for shops. I'm engaged to Hannah, who's a nursery assistant, and I owe about 34,000. My parents' shop only just pays its own bills, so there's nothing to borrow from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I expected. A lot of people talk about change before it comes, and most of the time it doesn't. I'd tell the men at church and at the shop that honest work still counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved but not at ease. The firms that hire embedded engineers are far away, in the industrial park forty miles from here, and I don't drive. I have a debt as big as three years of an entry salary, and the wedding keeps being pushed back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep working at the shop, and apply to Dunlop Tills and the six factories in the park. I'd ask my pastor, who knows the owners of two of them, to put in a word. I'd learn to drive, as well, because that's what's stopping me, and a lesson is 35.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. A little ashamed of being a burden at my age, though that's my own pride speaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was it like at Dunlop Tills, and could you go back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was good. They gave me a bench and a soldering iron, and I wrote code for a card reader's chip. The boss, Mr Dunlop, said to come back when I'd finished. But he has four engineers and one retired this year, and that's the only space I know about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do your plans with Hannah fit into the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We wanted to marry next June. It costs money, and neither family can contribute much. We'd probably have a small ceremony at church and a meal at my mother's table. Hannah says it's the marriage that counts, not the party, and she's right.

say: I'd tell the men at church that **honest work** still counts for something.
I'd say people talk about change before it comes, and often it doesn't.
think: I'd be relieved but not at ease: the firms are **forty miles** away and I don't drive.
My **34,000 debt** is three years of an entry salary and the wedding keeps getting pushed back.
do: Apply to **Dunlop Tills** and six factories in the industrial park, with my pastor's word.
Learn to **drive**, at 35 a lesson, since distance is the real problem.
feel: **Steady**, though a little ashamed of being a burden at my age.
S0.quote: I have a debt as big as three years of an entry salary, and the wedding keeps being pushed back.
fieldNote: Femi's worry is **distance and debt**, not technology; he doesn't drive and the factories are forty miles away.
He relies on his pastor's network rather than online applications.
The wedding with Hannah is already delayed by money.

steps.text: Apply to Dunlop Tills and six factories in the industrial park
Keep unloading deliveries at my parents' shop each morning
Plan a small church wedding for next June with Hannah

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful. New things promise a lot, and the people who profit tell us not to worry. I'd say jobs and families matter more than clever machines, and I'd say it plainly to anyone who asked at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it hits people like me hard. The easy part of my job, the writing of standard code, is what these tools do best, and a small firm like Dunlop Tills would keep two engineers instead of four. I'd be the one who's let go before I'm even hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study harder and become one of the people who knows the equipment, the hardware, which no tool can touch. I'd offer to work as an apprentice for less pay, if a firm would take me. I'd still avoid the AI tools themselves, because I've never trusted them and I don't want to depend on something I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit angry. I was told if you work hard and learn a skill, you'll be fine. Now I'm not sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would AI do to a job like a small firm's embedded engineer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two small firms near the industrial park do hardware repair and installation. I'd go to them in person with a cheap offer: a six-month apprenticeship, paid by the hour. I'd rather be useful for little than idle for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd keep refusing, for now. Maybe that's stubborn. My friend Josiah (a classmate) uses them all the time and he's quicker than me, I admit. But I'd rather know my own work first.

say: I'd say jobs and families matter more than **clever machines**, and the people who profit tell us not to worry.
I'd say it plainly at church.
think: The standard code I write is what these tools do best, so I'd be let go **before I'm hired**.
A small firm would keep **two engineers** instead of four.
do: Offer a **six-month apprenticeship** at an hourly wage to two hardware firms near the park.
Learn the **hardware**, which no tool can touch.
feel: **Uneasy**, a bit angry, since working hard and learning a skill no longer feels enough.
S1.quote: I'd rather be useful for little than idle for long.
fieldNote: Femi turns to **apprenticeship**, in line with his traditional view of work over handouts.
He admits his refusal of AI may be stubborn, citing his quicker classmate Josiah.
His sense of broken promise (work hard, be fine) is strong.

steps.text: Visit two hardware repair firms near the park and offer a paid apprenticeship
Take an extra hardware module in the master's, working on real boards
Wait until a firm I apply to actually uses these tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we must slow down and hold on to what matters: family, church and honest work. I'd say that out loud, in the shop and in church. A machine that can do all our thinking is not worth much if it leaves us without bread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm afraid. In two years, I'd be done with the course and holding a certificate for work the machines do better. I'd owe 34,000 with no job and a fiancée who depends on a nursery wage. I couldn't see how to go forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take whatever work comes, in the shop, at a farm, anywhere. I'd go to the pastor and the men's group about practical help, because the church has helped others before. I'd postpone the wedding again, with Hannah's blessing, and talk to the university about the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray more, and sleep less. It would feel like standing in a field with no fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have to delay. I couldn't marry her and ask her to share debt I can't pay. She'd say it doesn't matter, but I'd mind. A man should be able to provide, and I wouldn't be able to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father, my pastor and Hannah. Not the government, honestly. I'd take help from family and the church before an office. That may be pride, but it's how I was raised, and I'd try to keep it.

say: I'd say we must hold on to **family and church**.
I'd say a machine that does our thinking is not worth much if we're left without bread.
think: In two years I'd hold a certificate for work the machines do better, owing **34,000**.
My fiancée would depend on a **nursery wage**, and I couldn't see a way forward.
do: Take **any work**, at the shop or on a farm, and ask the pastor for practical help.
**Postpone** the wedding again with Hannah's blessing.
feel: **Frightened**, praying more and sleeping less, like standing in a field with no fence.
S2.quote: A machine that can do all our thinking is not worth much if it leaves us without bread.
fieldNote: Femi turns to **family and church** before any office, a pride he names himself.
The delayed wedding is tied to his idea of being a provider.
This is his worst scenario, with no plan beyond taking any work.

steps.text: Ask the pastor and men's group about practical help and work
Postpone the wedding again until I have steady pay
Take farm or warehouse work near Chapel Street
Stop all spending except rent share and loan minimum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for families and churches to prepare. I'd say to look after one another and not wait for government. I'd say to put away food, savings and skills, and to keep your faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a chance. I'd finish, take a job and have a few years of pay before the thinking work goes. After 2031 I'd expect to be doing something hands-on, not code. I'd guess most things will need a person to switch them on, fix them and answer for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first embedded job I could, even far away, and rent a room in the industrial park. I'd put 150 a month against the loan and 50 into savings for the wedding. I'd take an electrician's evening course too, since wires and machines always need someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious, but hopeful. There's a way, I think, and that's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the answer change with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd marry Hannah. We'd do it small and not wait for money to be perfect. I'd rather start our life with a plan than put it off for a fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also learn to drive, and finally. A licence is worth more than another certificate in this world.

say: I'd say five years is long enough for **families and churches** to prepare, so look after one another.
I'd tell people to put away food, savings and skills.
think: I'd have a few years of **pay** before the thinking work goes.
After 2031 I'd expect to do something **hands-on**, because machines still need someone to answer for them.
do: Take the first **embedded job** even far away, and rent a room in the industrial park.
Put **150 a month** on the loan and 50 toward the wedding.
feel: **Cautious but hopeful**, glad there is a way.
S3.quote: A licence is worth more than another certificate in this world.
fieldNote: Femi uses the extra time to **start his life**: job, loan, wedding.
He plans for a hands-on future and an electrician's course.
He wants to marry Hannah in the first year and not wait for perfect money.

steps.text: Take the first embedded job offered and rent a room near the park
Put 150 a month on the loan and 50 toward the wedding
Join an evening electrician's course at the technical college
Marry Hannah in a small church ceremony in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be patient. Ten years lets people raise their children, pay their debts and learn something new. I'd tell younger ones to learn a trade or two and keep their feet on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm. I'd marry, have a job and be a father, perhaps, by 2036. I'd expect to keep my hands busy, and my head too. The thinking AI would change things, but there'd be time to learn it, even for a slow learner like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job, then a second. I'd pay off the loan by about 30 and put a deposit on a small house near Chapel Street. I'd teach myself the new tools when I must, because by then everyone will need to. And I'd teach the young ones at church what I know about machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At peace, mostly. A little wistful, because things always change faster than I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years change about how you plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my father that my parents' shop will outlast the machines, because people still need bread and a friendly face. And that I'd take it over when he's ready, if the work goes elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I should do what I think is right. He's a man of few words, and I'm becoming like him.

say: I'd say it's a good time to be **patient**, and younger ones should learn a trade or two.
I'd tell them to keep their feet on the ground.
think: Privately I'd be **calm**: married, working and perhaps a father by 2036.
There'd be time to learn the new tools, even for a **slow learner**.
do: Take a first job, then a second, and clear the loan by about **30**.
Put a **deposit** on a small house near Chapel Street.
feel: **At peace**, a little wistful at how fast things change.
S4.quote: My parents' shop will outlast the machines, because people still need bread and a friendly face.
fieldNote: Femi's ten-year view is **settled** and family-centred, with the shop as an anchor.
He accepts he will learn the tools in time, as a slow learner.
His father is a man of few words, which he says he is becoming.

steps.text: Take the first embedded job, then move on after two years
Clear the loan by around age 30
Put a deposit on a small house near Chapel Street
Learn the new tools once my team starts using them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. It leaves no time and I'd owe all this money with nothing to show for it. What would help is an apprenticeship scheme that pays, a way to clear the loan by working, and employers who give a young man a start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't like being asked how I feel, but it helped. I think most people my age feel the same and say nothing. A man should be able to say he's afraid, and I'm learning that.

headlineQuote: A man should be able to say he's afraid, and I'm learning that.
portrait: Femi is 24, doing an **embedded systems master's** after software engineering, with 34,000 of debt and no savings.
He lives above his parents' grocery, helps unload crates, and is engaged to Hannah, a nursery assistant, though the wedding keeps slipping.
He is traditional, trusts church and family, **never uses AI**, and wants paid apprenticeships over handouts.
His moods run anxious in most worlds and alarmed at two years, easing to uneasy with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which leaves him owing money with nothing to show.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **paid apprenticeship** scheme, a way to clear the loan by working and employers who give young people a start.
